thread.title: David Einhorn Is Ditching Tech Stocks in Favor of Retail Stocks

author: Mary Childs
title: David Einhorn Is Ditching Tech Stocks in Favor of Retail Stocks
text:
By Mary Childs Updated Aug. 14, 2018 3:21 p.m. ET David Einhorn 's Greenlight Capital sold tech stocks in the second quarter to buy shares of retail companies, according to its most recent public filing of its holdings.
In the second quarter, Greenlight bought shares of Gap Inc. (GPS), Best Buy Co. (BBY), Dollar General Corp. (DG), Dollar Tree Stores (DLTR), and The TJX Companies (TJX), which runs T.J. Maxx, according to the filing . Greenlight traded one automotive seating company for another, paring its stake in Adient (ADNT), and buying shares of AutoZone (AZN). It trimmed holdings of Micron Technology (MU) and cut, by 77%, its holdings of Apple (AAPL), a position built up in 2016.
The filing is a snapshot of the fund's holdings at that moment in time, and are obviously subject to change. They also do not show short positions. So it's an imperfect picture of Einhorn and Greenlight's investing thesis.
Extrapolating from the available data, Greenlight is betting on consumers. Despite its difficulty sniffing out good investments in the past few years — The Wall Street Journal recently reported that Greenlight's flagship fund lost 18% this year through July, a sign that the market was saying it was "wrong, wrong, wrong about nearly everything," as Einhorn put it in a recent letter ) — the hedge fund may be onto something: There's a good case for retail right now.
David Einhorn, president of Greenlight Capital Inc., in 2015. Illustration: Andrew Harrer/Bloomberg Ben Levisohn wrote this weekend in the Barron's Trader column that outlook for the sector is brighter than it's been in a long time, with soaring consumer confidence and retailers cleaning up their portfolios of physical stores, helping margins. The SPDR S&P Retail ETF has climbed 35% since last year's low; last week it closed at a record high.
The National Retail Federation boosted its forecast for retail sales on Monday: The group now expects sales to increase by at least 4.5% over 2017, excluding automobiles, gasoline stations and restaurants. That's up from the range of 3.8% to 4.4% forecast earlier this year .
“Higher wages, gains in disposable income, a strong job market and record-high household net worth have all set the stage for very robust growth in the nation’s consumer-driven economy,” NRF President and CEO Matthew Shay said in a statement.
It's not perfectly directional — Greenlight also sold its holdings in Dillard's (DDS), shoe retailer DSW, discount chain Five Below (FIVE), Abercrombie & Fitch Co. (ANF), and Office Depot (ODP) -— but Greenlight's positioning appears to skew towards retailers targeting lower-income consumers. The fund also sold holdings in Urban Outfitters (URBN) and Tapestry (TPR), which owns Coach New York, Kate Spade New York, and Stuart Weitzman — higher price-point brands that need disposable income and probably a good swath of aspirational, upwardly-mobile consumers.
This might make sense on a few fronts — there are more jobs are open than workers seeking them as the U.S. finds itself in the midst of a labor crunch . Those conditions should have generated wage gains, yet so far they've been anemic. Consumers haven't felt much benefit from the strong economy. But in recent years, the unemployment rate for workers 25 years and up, with less than a high-school degree, have dropped precipitously, to 5.5% in June from 8.5% in September of 2016. That might be good news in particular for discount retailers, as Americans still recovering from the recession work their way back to financial health.
After some consternation earlier this year that consumers were stretched too thin, consumer sentiment appears to be holding in at high levels. Despite expectations for higher inflation and interest rates this year, and with caveats about any impact from tariffs and trade wars, households remain pretty confident, thanks to a good outlook for jobs and incomes. The University of Michigan's consumer sentiment index hit 97.9 in July, the lowest in six months but higher than the historic average of 86.35 from 1952 through 2018.
There's some divergence in economic outlook by age cohorts, according to Bank of America Merrill Lynch economists Michelle Meyer , Joseph Song , and Anna Zhou . Millennials are the least optimistic, according to the bank's survey: Just 39% of millennial respondents, and just 40% of Gen Xers, predict the U.S. economy will improve in the next 12 months, as of July. For baby boomers, that figure is 48%.
This comes as hedge funds bet that the death of malls is overblown, and just a year after hedge fund bets against brick-and-mortar retailers reached financial-crisis-era highs, according to a CNBC report on Bespoke Investment Group data.
The history of famous hedge funds investing in retail is not a proud one. There's Eddie Lampert's famous and ongoing investment in Sears Holdings (SHLD), which has fallen from $85 in 2010 to $1.83 today. Or Bill Ackman's investment in J.C. Penney about five years ago, which cost his hedge fund Pershing Square hundreds of millions of dollars. His earlier bets on Borders Group and Target Corp ( TGT ) were also not winners.
Greenlight sold out of shares of Consol Energy (CEIX), and supermarket chain Sprouts Farmers Market (SFM), according to the filings, and sold Third Point favorite Paypal Holdings (PYPL). Greenlight trimmed its investments in pharmaceutical companies Mylan (MYL) and Perrigo Co. (PRGO), and cut holdings in aircraft leasing company AerCap (AER), Voya Financial (VOYA), and technology-led business process services Conduent (CNDT).
